title: Smt. Bitti vs Sh. Rupender Singh on 26 November, 2016
full_text: Smt. Bitti vs Sh. Rupender Singh on 26 November, 2016 IN THE COURT OF MS. SHUCHI LALER, SCJ CUM RC (SHAHDARA) KKD COURTS, DELHI. RC / ARC No. 445/2016 In the matter of: Smt. Bitti W/o Sh Govind R/o H-2/2-C, Pocket-H-9, Dilshad Garden, Delhi- 110095 .... Petitioner Versus Sh. Rupender Singh S/o Sh. Avtar Singh R/o H.No. 488/9-E, Pocket - E, Dilshad Garden, Delhi 110 095 Also at M/s Cell Mart, Shop No. H-9, Pocket - H, Situated at C.S.C. Dilshad Garden, Delhi - 110 095 .... Respondent Date of institution of petition : 08.09.2014 Final arguments heard on : 26.11.2016 Judgment announced on : 26.11.2016 RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 APPLICATION FOR EVICTION OF TENANT UNDER SECTION 14 (1) (a) DRC Act, 1958 . JUDGMENT : 1. Eviction in respect of one shop measuring 9' X 6'3'' forming part of property bearing no. H.No. 9, Pocket - H situated at C.S.C, Dilshad Garden, Delhi (henceforth referred to as tenanted shop) has been sought on the ground that the respondent / tenant had defaulted in payment of rent despite service of demand notice, hence, committed 'first default', as envisaged under Clause (a) to the proviso of sub-section (1) of Section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 (in short ' DRC Act '). PETITION 2. Brief narration of the facts as disclosed in the petition is as under: 2.1 That the petitioner purchase the aforesaid property from erstwhile owner Smt. Preeti Jain vide registered sale deed and at the time of its purchased, respondent was in possession of the tenanted shop. 2.2 That the erstwhile owner had informed the petitioner RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 that she had allowed the respondent to run the tenanted shop without any lease or license fee as he was having cordial relations with family of erstwhile owner. 2.3 That the respondent failed to vacate the tenanted shop despite request of the erstwhile owner as well as petitioner, hence, the petitioner had to file a civil suit bearing no. 81/2012 against the respondent for recovery of possession and mesne profits. 2.4 That in the civil suit, the respondent filed his written statement wherein he had taken the plea that he was a tenant and had been paying rent at the rate of Rs.2,500/- per month excluding other charges. 2.5 That during the pendency of the civil suit, the respondent had sent a letter dated 18.05.2013 along with cheque bearing no. 042292 dated 04.05.2013 for a sum of Rs.50,000/- claiming it to be rent from 01.08.2011 to 30.04.2013. 2.6 That the petitioner did not encash the said cheque as the civil suit was pending adjudication. The civil suit was returned by the court of Sh. Amitabh Rawat, Ld. Civil Judge vide order dated 05.04.2013 on the ground of lack of pecuniary jurisdiction. 2.7 That the petitioner accepted the respondent as her tenant since 01.08.2011 and vide legal notice dated 10.06.2014 asked the respondent to pay rent w.e.f. 01.08.2011 till date. 2.8 That the legal notice was sent through speed post and registered A/D. The speed post was returned with the report of refusal on 14.06.2014 and registered A/D bears the endorsement RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 'the recipient has left the house'. Being aggrieved, the petitioner filed the present petition. WRITTEN STATEMENT 3. Written statement has been filed on behalf of the respondent wherein he has taken preliminary objections such as petitioner has concealed and misrepresented material facts and petitioner had no cause of action in his favour. The averments to the contrary made by the respondent are as under :- 3.1 That there are two tenants in the same shop. 1/4th (approx.) of shop no. H-9, Pocket -H, Dilshad Garden, Delhi is under the tenancy of respondent at monthly rent of Rs.2,500/- and 3/4th portion is under tenancy of another tenant namely Sh. Sushil Kumar Gupta who is still occupying the same. 3.2 That a mortgage agreement dated 04.01.2010 was executed between erstwhile owner Smt. Preeti Jain and the other tenant Mr. Sushil Kumar Gupta which has been concealed by the petitioner. 3.3 That no statutory notice was served upon the respondent. On 15.10.2014, the respondent made payment of arrears of rent from 01.08.2011 to 31.12.2014 @ Rs.2,500/- per month for 41 months totaling to Rs.82,500/- vide cheque no. 000059, dated 14.10.2014 drawn on HDFC Bank. RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 In view thereof, the respondent has alleged that the petitioner is not entitled for any relief and prayed for dismissal of the present petition with heavy cost. REPLICATION 4. Replication was duly filed on behalf of the petitioner wherein contrary averments were denied and the corresponding averments made in the petition were reiterated and reaffirmed as true and correct. ORDER UNDER SECTION 15 (1) DRC ACT 5. Ld. Predecessor, vide order dated 29.05.2015, directed the respondent to pay the rent @ Rs.2,500/- per month w.e.f. January, 2015 till date and further directed the respondent to pay future rent by 15th of every succeeding month. PETITIONERS' EVIDENCE 6. In support of his case, the petitioner stepped into the witness box as PW 1. He has tendered his evidence by way of affidavit which is Ex.PW1/A. PW-1 has relied upon the following documents:- ➢ Photocopy of Sale Deed as Ex. PW1/1 ➢ Site Plan Ex. PW1/2 RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 ➢ Photocopy of Written Statement filed by respondent in the CS No.- 81/12 as Ex. PW1/3 ➢ Photocopy of Letter dt. 18.05.2013 as Ex. PW1/4 ➢ Photocopy of envelope as Ex. PW1/5 ➢ Photocopy of cheque dt. 04.05.2013 as Ex. PW1/6 ➢ Certified copy of the order dt. 05.04.2014 in CS no. - 81/12 as Ex. PW1/7; ➢ Photocopy of Legal Notice as Ex. PW1/8; ➢ Postal Receipts (four in number) as Ex. PW1/9(colly.); ➢ Returned Envelops (four in number) as Ex. PW1/10 (colly.). The aforesaid witness was duly cross-examined by ld. counsel for respondent. Thereafter, the petitioner closed his evidence closed. RESPONDENT'S EVIDENCE 7. In rebuttal, the respondent stepped into the witness box as RW-1 and he has tendered his evidence by way of affidavit which is Ex.RW1/A. He has relied upon the cheque bearing no. 042292 as Ex. RW1/1. RW-1 was duly cross-examined by ld. counsel for petitioner. Thereafter, the respondent's evidence was closed. RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 FINAL ARGUMENTS 8. Rival submissions advanced at bar have been heard and record perused with the assistance of Ld. Counsels for parties. JUDICIAL RESOLUTION 9. In order to be entitled to an eviction order under clause (a) of sub section 1 of Section 14 of DRC Act, the petitioners are required to prove : (1). Relationship of landlord and tenant; (2). Existence of arrears of rent legally recoverable as on date of service of demand notice; (3). Service of notice of demand; (4). Failure of the tenant to pay / tender the entire legally recoverable arrears of rent within stipulated period of two months from the date of service of demand notice. 10. In the instant petition, the jural relationship of landlord - tenant and the rate of rent being Rs.2,500/- per month stands admitted. The points for adjudication are (i) the period since when the respondent is in arrears of rent; (ii) service of demand notice and (iii) whether respondent has complied with the mandate of the legal demand notice. RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 ARREARS OF RENT 11. First and foremost, the period since when the respondent is in arrears of rent needs to be ascertained. The petitioner has stated that the respondent has not paid the rent since 01.08.2011. The respondent has claimed that he has made payment of arrears of rent from 01.08.2011 till 30.04.2013 by way of cheque dated 04.05.2013 Ex RW1/1 which petitioner failed to encash and he again made payment of rent from 01.08.2011 to 31.12.2011 by cheque of Rs 82,500/-. 12. In the case titled as Sukhanand Vs. IVth Additional District Judge, Bulendshahar & Ors. 1994 (2) RCR (Rent) 408 it has been held that the onus to show payment of rent lies on the tenant and oral testimony of tenant in regard to the payment of rent claiming discharge of liability in this regard cannot be admitted to be worth reliance at all. 13. Similar view has been reiterated in the case titled as Raghubir Prasad Vs. Rajendra Kumar Gurudev , 1993(2) R.C.R. (Rent) 234, wherein it has been held that on default in payment of rent, the onus to show payment of rent lies on tenant. Further, in the case of Satya Prakash Vs. District Judge Ghaziabad , 1982(1) R.C.R. (Rent) 295, it was observed that if in a petition, tenant alleges that rent is paid, then as per Evidence Act , burden to prove payment lies on the tenant, as he alleges that payment is made. RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 14. Reference can also be made to the judgment titled as Karamchand Deojee Sanghavi Vs. Tulshiram Kalu Kumawat , 1992(1) RCR 118 wherein the Hon'ble Bombay High Court observed that in a case of eviction on arrears of rent, the onus would always be on tenant to prove that he has paid the rent. 15. Thus, in the instant case, the onus was upon the respondent / tenant to prove that he has made payment of rent regularly and there were no arrears of rent due against him as claimed in the legal demand notice Ex.PW1/8. The respondent/RW1 has deposed that he made payment of rent from 1.8.2011 till 30.04.2013 by way of cheque dated 0422292 drawn on HDFC Bank Ex RW1/1, however, the petitioner had not encashed the same. The questions which have arisen before the court are as under:- (A) Whether tendering of rent by cheque is a valid tender? (B) Whether the respondent was legally required to deposit rent in court under section 27 of Delhi Rent Control Act if the cheque Ex RW1/1 was admittedly not encashed? (A) Whether tendering of rent by cheque is a valid tender? 16 Tendering of rent by cheque is a valid tender of rent and it has been so held by Honorable Delhi High Court in a judgment titled as Arun Kumar Gupta Vs Rakesh Sood 187(2012) DLT 267. In the said judgment the Honorable High Court relied upon a judgment of the Apex Court titled Mahender RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 Raghunathdas Gupta Vs Vishwanath Mogul AIR 1997 SC 2437 in which it was observed that tender of rent by cheque is a valid tender unless it is specifically mentioned that the payment must be in cash. (B) Whether the respondent was legally required to deposit rent in court under section 27 of Delhi Rent Control Act if the cheque Ex RW1/1 was not encashed? 17. The next question which arises for consideration is whether due to admitted non encashment of the said cheque Ex RW1/1, the repondent was under a legal obligation to deposit the rent under section 27 of Delhi Rent Control Act. Honorable Supreme Court in judgment titled as Sarla Goel Vs Kishan Chand 2009 (7) SCC 658 observed as under:- "4. The facts are not in dispute. The respondent is a tenant in respect of the suit premises. As noted herein earlier, it is not disputed that the respondent has already availed of the benefit of Section 14(2) read with Section 15 of the Act pursuant to an order dated 3rd of December, 2001 passed by the Additional Rent Controller, Delhi in Eviction Case No. E-105 of 1999. At the present juncture, it may be mentioned that the appellants is now facing the charge of committing second default in payment of rent to the appellants in respect of the suit premises. It is also not in dispute that a demand notice dated 31st of March, 2003 was served by the appellants upon the respondent intimating that the respondent was in arrears of rent for three consecutive months from January, 2003 onwards. It is also not in dispute that on receipt of the said demand notice from the appellants, the respondent had sent the arrears of rent for three months for the period from 1st of January, 2003 to 31st of March, 2003 by a money order dated 22nd of April, 2003. It is also not in dispute that the appellants had refused to accept the money order and consequently, the RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 money was refunded to the respondent. The case made out by the respondent was that he had duly complied with the provisions of the Act which was required to be done by him and therefore, it cannot be held that it was a case of second default whereas the case of the appellants either before the Rent Controller or before the High Court was that on refusal to receive the money order by the appellants, the respondent ought to have taken the recourse of Section 27 of the Act by depositing the aforesaid arrears of rent with the Rent Controller and he not having admittedly done so, was liable to be evicted from the suit premises on the ground of second default under Section 14(1)(a) read with proviso to Section 14(2) of the Act. ....... 11. We are unable to accept this submission of the learned counsel for the tenant/respondent for the following reasons :- It is true that in Section 27 of the Act, it has been provided that the tenant may deposit rent when such rent was not accepted or refused or no receipt was granted by the landlord or there was bonafide doubt as to the person or the persons to whom the rent was payable, the tenant may deposit such rent with the Rent Controller in the prescribed manner. 12. Chapter III deals with Control of Eviction of Tenants. Section 14 gives a specific right to the tenants to resist evictions. Sub- section (2) of Section 14 of the Act provides that no order for recovery of possession of any premises shall be made on the grounds specified in Class A of the proviso to sub-section (1) if the tenant makes payment or deposit the rent as required by Section 15 . 13. An overall reading of Chapter III of the Act would clearly show that an additional protection has been given by the Legislature to the tenant who has committed default in payment of rent for which he is liable to be evicted under Section 14(1)(a) of the Act. Section 14(1)(a) of the Act clearly provides that when the tenant has neither paid nor tendered whole of the arrears of the rent legally recoverable from him within two months from the date of which a notice of payment of the arrears of rent has been served on him by the landlord in the manner provided in Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. A plain reading of sub- section (2) of Section 14 makes it clear that a tenant is protected from eviction if he makes payment or deposits the rent as required by Section 15 . Section 15 deals with cases when a tenant can get the benefit of protection against eviction. 14. Accordingly, Section 14(1)(a) is a ground for eviction of a tenant for default in payment of rent. In spite of that, RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 protection has been given under Section 15 of the Act to the tenant to avail of the protection given by the Legislature by depositing rent in the manner indicated in Section 15 of the Act. However, proviso to Section 14(2) of the Act takes away the right of a tenant of the benefit of Sub-Section (2) of Section 14 if the tenant having obtained such benefit once in respect of any premises and makes a further default in payment of rent of those premises for three consecutive months. Therefore, it has been made clear that when the tenant makes a second default, no protection can be given to the tenant from eviction. 15. Chapter IV, however, deals with Deposit of Rent. Section 26 of the Act provides that if the rent is paid it is the obligation of the landlord to grant receipt for the rent paid to him. In default of payment of rent within the time specified therein, the tenant is also liable to pay simple interest at the rate of 15% per annum from the date on which such payment of rent is due to the date on which it is paid. The proviso to Section 26(2) of the Act makes it clear that it shall be open to the tenant to remit the rent to his landlord by postal money order. Sub-section (3) of Section 26 also makes the provision that if the landlord or his authorized agent refuses or neglects to deliver to the tenant a receipt referred to in sub-section (2), the Controller may, on an application made to him in this behalf by the tenant within two months from the date of payment and after hearing the landlord or his authorized agent, by order direct the landlord or his authorized agent to pay to the tenant, by way of damages, such sum not exceeding double the amount of rent paid by the tenant and the costs of the application and shall also grant a certificate to the tenant in respect of the rent paid. From a reading of sub-section (3) of Section 26 of the Act, it is clear that the tenant has been given further protection to get the rent receipt from the landlord and in the event the landlord refuses to grant such receipt, the procedure has been clearly made by the Legislature for the purpose of getting the receipt under the Act and at the same time the landlord can be imposed to pay damages not exceeding double the amount paid by the tenant and the costs of the application and to obtain a certificate from the landlord in respect of the rent paid. Now we come to the most important provision regarding the procedure under the Act to pay or deposit or tender rent to the landlord, if he refuses to grant any receipt in respect of the payment already made to him. As quoted herein earlier, Section 27 deals with deposit of rent by the tenant. It clearly says that where the landlord does not accept any rent tendered by the tenant within the time referred to in Section 26 or RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 refuses or neglects to deliver a receipt referred to therein or where there is a bona fide doubt as the person or persons to whom the rent is payable, the tenant may deposit such rent with the Controller in the prescribed manner. When the words 'bona fide doubt' has been added to Section 27 , the tenant may remit such rent to the Controller by postal money order. From a conjoint reading of this provision referred to herein above and particularly Section 27 of the Act, in our view, it cannot be doubted that the procedure having been made by the Legislature how the rent can be deposited if it was refused to have been received or to grant receipt for the same. If that be the position, if such protection has been given to the tenant, the said procedure has to be strictly followed in the matter of taking steps in the event of refusal of the landlord to receive the rent or to grant receipt to the tenant. It is well settled that whether the word 'may' shall be used as 'shall', would depend upon the intention of the Legislature. It is not to be taken that once the word 'may' is used by the Legislature in Section 27 of the Act, would not mean that the intention of the Legislature was only to show that the provisions under Section 27 of the Act was directory but not mandatory. 16. In other words, taking into consideration the object of the Act and the intention of the Legislature and in view of the discussions made herein earlier, we are of the view that the word 'may' occurring in Section 27 of the Act must be construed as a mandatory provision and not a directory provision as the word 'may' , in our view, was used by the Legislature to mean that the procedure given in those provisions must be strictly followed as the special protection has been given to the tenant from eviction. Such a cannon of construction is certainly warranted because otherwise intention of the Legislature would be defeated and the class of landlords, for whom also, the beneficial provisions have been made for recovery of possession from the tenants on certain grounds, will stand deprived of them." 18. From the aforesaid judgment it is clear that if the landlord refuses to accept rent, then the tenant is required to deposit rent in court under section 27 of Delhi Rent Control Act and in case he does not deposit rent in the court, then he cannot claim protection from eviction under section 14(1)(a) of Delhi RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 Rent Control Act . 19. Thus, in the present case, the respondent had the knowledge that the cheque had not been encashed by the petitioner as the cheque expired after six months from 04.05.2013 and after the expiration of period of six months, the respondent could have deposited the rent in court under section 27 of Delhi Rent Control Act but the respondent did not do so and waited for the filing of the present petition. The facts of the present case are squarely covered by the judgment of Sarla Goel (Supra). The respondent was under a legal obligation to deposit rent in court under section 27 of Delhi Rent Control Act, but, the respondent failed to discharge the said obligation. 20. At the cost of repetition, it is reiterated that the respondent has claimed that he had sent the arrears of rent from 01.08.2011 till 31.12.2014 by way of cheque of Rs 82,500/-dated 14.10.2014. The said contention is itself an admission of the fact that as on the date of notice Ex.PW-1/8 i.e. 10.06.2014, the respondent was in arrears of rent with effect from 1.8.2011. Had the respondent not been in arrears of rent, he had no reason to send the payment of arrears of rent through cheque dated 14.10.2014.Thus, the respondent is held to be in arrears of rent w.e.f 01.08.2011 till 30.04.2013. SERVICE OF LEGAL NOTICE 21. Another contentious issue is the service of demand notice dated 10.06.2014 Ex.PW1/8 upon the respondent as it is RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 the service of the demand notice which is precursor to present petition under Section 14 (1) (a) DRC Act. 22. The petitioner had sent legal notice dated 10.06.2014 Ex.PW-1/8 through Speed Post and Registered AD Ex.PW1/9. One of the Registered Envelop Ex.PW1/10 sent to residential address of respondent has been received with the report of refusal.The respondent, in the written statement, denied the service of legal notice. 23. In the opinion of the court, the legal notice was duly served upon the respondent for the following reasons:- (A) Firstly, because there is a presumption of service as per Section 114 of Evidence Act and Section 27 of General Clauses Act as the Legal Notice Ex.PW1/8 was sent through Registered Post. In K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan, (SC ) 1 11999 A.I.R. (SC) 3762 : 1999 Cri.L.J. 4606 : 1999(4) Crimes 212 : 1999(7) S.C.C. 510 : 1999(7) J.T. 558 Apex Court observe as under as regards service of notice sent by post:­ "22. It is well settled that a notice refused to be accepted by the addressee can be presumed to have been served on him, [Vide Harchan Singh v. Smt. Shivarani and Ors., 1981( 2) SCC 535, and Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh , 1992(1) SCC 647]. 23. Here the notice is returned as unclaimed and not as refused. Will there be any significant difference between the two so far as the presumption of service is concerned ? In this connection a reference to Section 27 of the General Clauses Act will be useful. The Section reads thus : "27. Meaning of service by post.­ Where any central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression "serve" or either of the expressions "give" or "send" or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, pre­paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post." 24. No doubt Section 138 of the Act does not require that the notice should be given only by "post". Nonetheless the principle incorporated in Section 27 (quoted above) can profitably be imported in a case where the sender has despatched the notice by post with the correct address written on it. Then it can be deemed to have been served on the sendee unless he proves that it was not really served and that he was not responsible for such non­service. Any other interpretation can lead to a very tenuous position as the drawer of the cheque who is liable to pay the amount would resort to the strategy of subterfuge by successfully avoiding the notice. 25. Thus, when a notice is returned by the sendee as unclaimed such date would be the commencing date in reckoning the period of 15 days contemplated in clause (d) to the proviso of Section 138 of the Act. Of course such reckoning would be without prejudice to the right of the drawer of the cheque to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address. In the present case the accused did not even attempt to discharge the burden to rebut the aforesaid presumption." RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 it was observed by Honorable Apex Court that the principle incorporated in Section 27 can profitably be imported in a case where the sender has dispatched the notice by post with the correct address written on it. Then it can be deemed to have been served on the sendee unless he proves that it was not really served and that he was not responsible for such non-service. It was further observed that when a notice is returned by the sendee as unclaimed such date would be the commencing date in reckoning the period of 15 days contemplated in clause (d) to the proviso of Section 138 of the Act. The said judgment was relied upon by Full Bench of Honorable Apex Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed, (SC ) 2007 (3) RCR (Criminal) 185 and it was observed that when a notice is sent by registered post and is returned with a postal endorsement "refused" or "not available in the house" or "house locked" or "shop closed" or "addressee not in station", due service has to be presumed. Thus, Service of legal demand notice Ex.PW1/4 stands proved as per Section 114 of Evidence Act and Section 27 of General Clauses Act as the same was sent through registered post and was received with the report of refusal. (B) Secondly, the address of respondent as mentioned in Legal Notice Ex.PW-1/8 and the registered post received with report of refusal Ex. PW-1/10 is correct . This fact has been admitted by RW-1, in his cross examination, when he stated his residential address to be 488/9-E, Pocket E, Dilshad Garden, RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 Delhi 95 which is the same address as mentioned in legal notice as well as registered envelope. (C) Thirdly, in order to rebut the presumption under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act and section 27 of General Clauses Act, the respondent had to lead cogent evidence. Except the bald denial of the respondent, no evidence in rebuttal has been led to show non service of the demand notice. Thus, the court is of the opinion that the Legal Notice Ex.PW-1/8 was duly served upon the respondent. VALID TENDER OF ARREARS OF RENT 24. Lastly, coming to the aspect whether within two months of service of notice, the rent has been validly tendered or paid for the period in dispute by the respondent. 25. The report of refusal on the registered envelope Ex PW1/10 is 14.06.2014. Thus,the respondent is deemed to have been served with the demand notice on 14.06.2014. The arrears of rent have been sent to the petitioner by way of cheque dated 14.10.2014. It is apparent that the respondent has not made payment of arrears of rent within two months from the date of service of legal notice i.e 14.06.2014. 26. Ld Counsel for respondent strenuously urged that the instant petition is liable to be dismissed as PW1 has admitted, in his cross examination, that the respondent is not in arrears of rent, thus, the instant petition is without any cause of action. RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 27. The relevant extract of cross-examination which has been strongly relied upon by Ld Counsel for respondent is reproduced hereinbelow:- "...... My wife has received full rent from the respondent till date and nothing is due..........It is correct that no rent is due from respondent qua suit shop up to date....." 28. The testimony of a witness has to be read as a whole and in toto. It can not be split up and part of it being used against the petitioner. It is not to be ignored that on first page of his cross- examination, PW1 also stated that he does not remember the date, month and year from which respondent has not paid rent but then he volunteered and stated that respondent has not paid rent for last 2 ½ - 3 years. An admission is required to be clear, unqualified and unambiguous. The court can not extract and read only that part of PW1 testimony which is favorable to his adversary. The evidence has to be read as a whole. Moreover, by and large the aspect of valid tender of rent is based on documentary evidence in the instant eviction petition with oral evidence assuming least significance. Further, a common man is unaware of nuances of law. Maybe PW1 stated that entire rent has been paid for the reason that the cheque of arrears of rent was undoubtedly sent by respondent but PW1, being a common man having no legal knowledge, can not be presumed to know whether it was a valid tender or not. Thus, this contention of respondent is without merits and is rejected. RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 INTEREST 29. Ld Counsel for petitioner contended that the interest component is missing in the alleged rent sent from 01.08.2011 to 30.04.2013 by cheque bearing no.00059 of Rs.82,500/- drawn on HDFC Bank. He submitted that as per section 26 of Delhi Rent Control Act, the respondent is liable to pay interest on rent due in case the respondent does not pay rent regularly by the 15 th of succeeding month. In the present case admittedly the respondent had not paid rent by 15th of each succeeding month and as such he was under a statutory obligation to tender interest along with rent, which he failed to tender. 30. In the judgment titled as Arun Kumar Gupta Vs Rakesh Sood 187(2012) DLT 267 Honorable Delhi High Court observed as under:- "7. Record has been perused. Record shows that in the legal notice there has been no demand of interest; the legal notice has made a demand of rent for three months to be paid within two months without detailing any dates. It is an admitted fact that within one week of the receipt of the legal notice Rs. 8,400/- was tendered by way of the aforenoted cheque which was at the admitted rate of rent for a period of 14 years although contention of the tenant is that the legally recoverable rent is only three years preceding the filing of the eviction petition. That apart, since there was no demand for the rent to be paid alongwith interest, the judgment of Raghbir Singh (supra) would not be applicable. In the case of Raghbir Singh (supra) the legal notice had specifically made a demand of arrears of rent specifying details of the arrears of rent alongwith interest to be paid under Section 26 of DRCA which had not been tendered......." (emphasis supplied) RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 31. The present case is squarely covered by the aforesaid judgment as even in the demand notice Ex PW1/8, no interest has been demanded, only the respondent has been asked to make payment of arrears of rent. As such the respondent was under no obligation to tender interest on arrears of rent. 32. Be that as it may, as discussed hereinabove, the respondent has not made payment of arrears of rent within stipulated period of two months from the date of service of legal notice. CONCLUSION Keeping in view the foregoing reasons and discussion, the court is of the opinion that the petitioner has successfully established the ground under Section 14 (1) (a) DRC Act. However, as per the provisions of DRC Act , in case a tenant is evicted for non-payment of rent U/s 14 (1) (a) DRC Act , he has to be given a chance for payment of arrears of rent so as to enable him to avail the benefit U/s 14 (2) DRC Act . Therefore, as per the provisions of Section 15(1) DRC Act, the respondent is directed to pay arrears of rent @ Rs.2,500/- per month w.e.f. 01.08.2011 till date along with interest @ 15% per annum as per section 26 of the DRC Act within a period of one month from today after adjusting the rent which has already been deposited / paid in the Court. The respondent shall RC / ARC No. : 445/2016 Bitti vs. Rupender Singh Page No. of 21 continue to make payment of future rent by 15 th of each succeeding month. The main file be consigned to Record Room and Ahlmad is directed to maintain a separate miscellaneous file for the purpose of consideration of benefit U/s 14 (2) DRC Act . Put up on 20.02.2017 for consideration of benefit U/s 14 (2) DRC Act . Copy of this judgment be also kept in the separate miscellaneous file.
